Blackfoot

This wider Blackfoot route concerns the Siksikaitsitapi Confederacy and its constituent peoples, including Siksika, Kainai, Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni. It begins with a Siksika-produced public book and the Confederacy Council's account, while keeping the Montana Blackfeet Nation distinct from the whole Confederacy.

One substantial community-produced book, inspected in selected relevant pages, supports an initial Confederacy and language route. Two short official pages supply scoped institutional/identity context only. Coverage across the four nations remains uneven.

Assessment recorded October 27, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • This is a brief Confederacy route with one selected Siksika publication; substantial Kainai, Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni community histories and authors remain to be reviewed.
  • Selected pages of the 2020 book were inspected. Its other sections, underlying oral recordings, specialist language scholarship and cited historical works remain unread.
  • The 2000 declaration itself and original Canadian and United States treaties were not examined; no current legal, boundary or membership conclusion follows from the Council's summary.
  • No Blackfoot community review or endorsement is recorded. The photograph shows one dated Montana conservation activity, not the entire Confederacy.

Copy the existing cleared USDA NRCS photograph and all its credits/rights without changing the old mapping. The Council explicitly identifies Aamskapi Pikuni as the Montana Blackfeet Nation, a constituent of the wider Confederacy. Display the photograph as the specifically captioned Blackfeet Tribal conservation activity in 2012; it does not depict all Confederacy nations, establish every participant's citizenship or prove current ecological outcomes. The NRCS caption specifically identifies Anne Stephens as Blackfeet Tribal Conservationist and names producers Gus Vaile and Lester Gray placing a range-monitoring square on the Blackfeet Reservation. This supplies an individually scoped institutional and place connection to the Montana government. It does not establish the citizenship of every participant or represent all Blackfeet or the whole Confederacy. The photograph documents a particular 2012 activity; present land conditions, ecological outcomes and personal viewpoints are not inferred. Identity and context

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Kainai, Siksika, Piikani and Blackfeet communities; language and confederacy relationships. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] blackfootconfederacy.ca

03

A Confederacy with distinct constituent nations

Stories of the Siksika identifies Siksika, Kainai and Piikani, including Piikani communities in Alberta and Montana. It describes shared language and cultural relationships alongside features particular to Siksika. The Confederacy Council's separate institutional history dates its declaration to May 2000 in Lethbridge. These sources distinguish collective relationships from the histories and governments of individual nations.

Read the sources [2] Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park; hosted by Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council [3] Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council

04

A Siksika publication on language and transmission

In the book's 2020 introduction, Stephen Yellow Old Woman explains the importance of passing history between generations through oral traditions. Its language chapter presents Siksika as one of four Blackfoot dialects and describes continuity together with vocabulary change. This is the Park's public Siksika account, rather than a full linguistic survey or permission to generalize one community's practices to every Blackfoot nation.

Read the sources [2] Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park; hosted by Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council

Stories of the Siksika (first printing March 2020) ↗

A Siksika-produced public book that places its own nation within the wider Confederacy and explains language continuity. The introduction by Stephen Yellow Old Woman frames the publication through intergenerational oral transmission. Selected introductory and language pages were read, not the complete volume or its cited works. The publisher retains content/image rights; none of its photographs or logos is reproduced here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual 41-spread PDF downloaded once. Read and visually inspected printed pp. 2–3 (acknowledgements, March 2020 first printing, rights and contents), 8–9 (self-description and Stephen Yellow Old Woman introduction), 14 (Confederacy and Clans) and 41 (Speaking Siksika), corresponding to PDF pp. 3, 6, 9 and 22. The adjacent printed pages were visible in those spreads but supply no proposed retelling of stories, ceremonial instruction or image reuse. Text extraction exposed additional pages; no whole-book review is claimed. Linked and cited works remain unread.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Our Mission & History — Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council ↗

The Council's short institutional account names four constituent peoples and dates the declaration to 25 May 2000 in Lethbridge. Useful supporting context for collective agency; its brief mission and declaration paragraph are not counted as a substantial independent work. Original declaration and treaties were not inspected.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Complete visible main body lines 16–50 read, including mission, values and the declaration paragraph. Names of leaders, current news, linked declarations, treaties and images were not used.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Our Lands & Tribes — Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council ↗

An official orientation naming Kainaiwa, Siksika, Apatosi Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni and identifying Aamskapi Pikuni with the Montana Blackfeet Nation. This identity and photo-context reference is excluded from the substantive reading count and starting guide. Undated population figures and sensitive-place descriptions are not adopted.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Actual council/constituent descriptions at lines 11–14, 22–24, 34–36, 45–47 and 56–58 read. Later sacred-place paragraph, video and linked nation websites supply no proposed claim; undated counts are omitted.
